question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Indiana?
body:
## Direct Answer
You find a fractional CRO in Indiana through five proven channels: fractional-executive marketplaces and networks, RevOps and sales consultancies with a Midwest bench, warm referrals from Indianapolis-area VCs and peer CEOs, targeted LinkedIn searches filtered to the state, and local professional communities like Pavilion with an active Midwest presence. Prioritize candidates who have carried a number in your specific motion — B2B SaaS, manufacturing, or services — over generalists, and validate them against a scorecard before signing.

Hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer is one of the highest-leverage moves a growth-stage Indiana company can make, but the search process is genuinely different from a full-time executive hire. You are buying pattern-matching and part-time bandwidth, not a permanent seat, so the sourcing channels, the vetting bar, and the engagement structure all shift. This guide walks the whole path — where to look, how to filter, what to pay attention to, and how to structure the relationship so a two-to-three-day-a-week leader actually moves your pipeline.

## What exactly is a fractional CRO and why would an Indiana company hire one?
A fractional CRO is an experienced revenue leader who owns your entire go-to-market engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, partnerships, and customer expansion — on a part-time, ongoing basis, typically one to three days a week under a multi-month contract. Unlike a full-time CRO who costs a mid-six-figure base plus equity, a fractional operates on a monthly retainer, so a company doing a few million in revenue can access executive-caliber leadership it otherwise could not justify. The role is distinct from a consultant: a consultant recommends, a fractional CRO executes, hires, forecasts, and carries accountability for the number.

For Indiana specifically, the fit is strong. The state's economy skews toward B2B manufacturing, logistics, agtech, insurance, life sciences, and a fast-maturing Indianapolis and Fishers software scene anchored by the legacy of companies like ExactTarget and Salesforce Marketing Cloud. Many of these firms are founder-led, profitable, and scaling past the point where the founder can personally run sales — the exact inflection where a fractional CRO earns their keep. Rather than gamble a full year of runway on a full-time hire who may not fit, an Indiana founder can bring in a seasoned operator to build the machine, install the process, hire the first real sales leader, and then step back. If you want the underlying framework for when this role pays off, see the deeper breakdown at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-roi-model.

![Where do I find a fractional CRO in Indiana — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9375-b1.jpg)


The second reason is talent geography. Indiana has a deep bench of enterprise sales and RevOps veterans who spent careers at Indianapolis-headquartered or Midwest-anchored companies and now want portfolio-style work instead of another full-time grind. That local supply means you can often find someone who understands the regional buyer, the talent pool you will recruit from, and the pace of Midwest B2B deals — an edge over a coastal fractional who has never sold into a Fort Wayne manufacturer.

## Where are the actual channels to find one in Indiana?
There are five channels that reliably surface qualified fractional CROs, and the best searches run several of them in parallel rather than betting on one. The first is **fractional-executive networks and marketplaces** — organizations that specifically vet and represent part-time C-suite operators. National networks like Chief Outsiders, Bespoke Partners' fractional bench, TechCXO, Go Fractional, and Continuum all place revenue leaders and can filter for someone Indiana-based or willing to work Central Time with occasional on-site visits. These platforms pre-screen for the fractional operating model, which saves you from candidates who really want a full-time seat in disguise.

![Where do I find a fractional CRO in Indiana — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9375-b2.jpg)


The second channel is **RevOps and sales consultancies with fractional practices.** Firms that do revenue operations, sales enablement, and GTM strategy frequently offer a fractional-CRO tier where a partner embeds with your team. The advantage is a bench behind the individual — if your fractional needs a Salesforce admin, a demand-gen specialist, or a comp-plan modeler for a week, the firm supplies it. The tradeoff is that you are buying a firm's methodology, so make sure it matches your motion. Our library covers how to evaluate these engagements at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-consultancy-vs-fractional.

The third and often highest-yield channel is **warm referrals.** Indiana's venture and operator community is tight. TechPoint (the state's tech-talent and ecosystem organization), Elevate Ventures, High Alpha and its studio network, and the Indianapolis chapters of founder groups like EO and Vistage all function as referral engines. A single email to a peer CEO who recently ran a fractional engagement will surface a better-qualified name than fifty cold LinkedIn messages. The fourth channel is **LinkedIn and direct search**, filtered to Indiana and to titles like "Fractional CRO," "Fractional VP Sales," and "GTM Advisor." The fifth is **local professional communities** — Pavilion (formerly Revenue Collective) has an active Midwest presence, and its members are almost exclusively revenue leaders, many of whom take fractional work.

![Where do I find a fractional CRO in Indiana — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9375-b3.jpg)


```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Start your fractional CRO search] --> B[Define motion and stage]
  B --> C[Run channels in parallel]
  C --> D[Fractional networks and marketplaces]
  C --> E[RevOps consultancies with fractional tier]
  C --> F[Warm referrals from Indiana VCs and peers]
  C --> G[LinkedIn filtered to Indiana]
  C --> H[Pavilion and operator communities]
  D --> I[Build shortlist of five candidates]
  E --> I
  F --> I
  G --> I
  H --> I
  I --> J[Score against fit rubric]
  J --> K[Reference and paid trial]
  K --> L[Sign structured engagement]
```

A practical sequencing note: start referrals and networks first because they take longest to bear fruit, then layer in your own LinkedIn sourcing while you wait. Running the channels concurrently compresses a search that would otherwise stretch across months into a few weeks. Aim to build a shortlist of at least five candidates before you fall in love with any single one — the discipline of comparison is what protects you from a charismatic generalist.

## Does the fractional CRO actually need to be in Indiana?
Not strictly, and this is where many founders over-constrain their search. The fractional model is inherently remote-friendly — most engagements run on video with periodic on-site visits — so a great operator in Chicago, Cincinnati, Columbus, or Louisville is well within a comfortable drive of most Indiana companies and shares the Central or Eastern-adjacent time zone and Midwest deal rhythm. Widening your radius to the broader Midwest roughly triples your candidate pool without meaningfully sacrificing on-site availability.

That said, there are real reasons to weight local. If your sales motion involves recruiting reps from the Indianapolis, Bloomington, or Lafayette talent markets, a locally networked CRO can pull candidates you cannot reach. If you sell into Indiana or regional buyers — manufacturers, hospital systems, ag operations, municipal contracts — someone who already knows those accounts and their buying cycles shortens ramp. And if your board or founder simply values in-person whiteboard sessions, proximity matters for culture. The right rule is: prefer Indiana or an adjacent metro when the motion is regional or recruiting-heavy, but do not disqualify a superb operator two states away when the motion is national and digital.

One caution on the fully-remote-anywhere option. A fractional CRO on the coasts selling you a Silicon Valley playbook can misjudge Midwest deal velocity, comp expectations, and the pace at which regional buyers move. That is not a hard no — plenty of coastal operators adapt well — but it is a specific thing to probe in references. Ask their prior clients whether the operator adjusted the playbook to the market or tried to force-fit a template.

## How do I vet and evaluate a fractional CRO candidate?
Vetting a fractional is more demanding than vetting a full-timer precisely because the engagement is short and the ramp is compressed — you do not have a year to discover a mistake. Build a scorecard before you take the first call so you are comparing candidates on the same axes rather than on charisma. Five dimensions matter most. **Relevant motion experience** — have they carried a quota and built a team in your specific model (SaaS subscription, manufacturing distribution, professional services, marketplace)? A CRO who scaled enterprise SaaS may be the wrong hire for a transactional SMB motion. **Stage fit** — building a repeatable process from near-zero is a different skill than optimizing a machine already doing real revenue; match the candidate's proven stage to yours.

The remaining three: **operating versus advising** — press for specifics on what they personally built and ran, not what they "advised on," because the fractional value is execution, not slideware. **References that reflect outcomes** — insist on speaking to two or three prior fractional clients and ask about pipeline built, hires made, and forecast accuracy, not just whether they were pleasant. And **cultural and communication fit** — a part-time leader who cannot get your team to follow them will accomplish nothing regardless of pedigree. Our full interview framework lives at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vetting-scorecard.

The single most reliable vetting tool is a **paid trial project** — a two-to-four-week scoped engagement where the candidate audits your pipeline, delivers a GTM diagnostic, and proposes a plan. This costs a fraction of a bad hire and reveals exactly how they think, how fast they move, and whether your team responds to them. A candidate who resists a paid trial is telling you something. The diagram below shows the funnel from raw sourcing down to signed engagement, and where the trial sits.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Twenty raw candidates] --> B[Screen for motion and stage fit]
  B --> C[Ten pass initial screen]
  C --> D[Structured interview on scorecard]
  D --> E[Five strong candidates]
  E --> F[Reference calls with prior clients]
  F --> G[Two finalists]
  G --> H[Paid trial diagnostic project]
  H --> I[One selected fractional CRO]
  I --> J[Structured engagement with clear scope]
```

Watch for specific red flags. Be wary of a candidate who has ten simultaneous fractional clients — the model works at two or three, but beyond that your company gets leftover attention. Be wary of anyone who promises a revenue number before they have seen your pipeline; a serious operator diagnoses before they prescribe. And be wary of a resume that is all advisory and board seats with no recent hands-on operating — the market moves, and a leader who has not personally run a modern sales stack in five years may be selling nostalgia.

## What should the engagement and pricing structure look like?
Fractional CRO engagements are almost always structured as a **monthly retainer** tied to a committed number of days or a defined scope, running on a multi-month term with a notice period on both sides. The exact rate varies widely by the operator's pedigree, the days-per-week commitment, and your company's complexity, so treat any single number you hear as a data point rather than a benchmark, and get quotes from several candidates to triangulate the market. The important discipline is not chasing the lowest retainer — a cheap fractional who cannot move the number is the most expensive hire you can make — but matching the investment to the outcome you need.

Structure the engagement around **clear, time-bound deliverables** rather than vague "leadership." A strong first ninety days usually includes a pipeline and forecast audit, a rebuilt or installed sales process, a fixed comp plan, a hiring plan for the roles the company actually needs, and a reporting cadence the founder and board can trust. Define what "done" looks like at thirty, sixty, and ninety days, and tie a portion of the relationship's continuation to hitting those milestones. Many engagements also include a **transition clause** — the fractional's ultimate job is often to build the machine and hire the full-time leader who will run it, then hand off cleanly. Naming that end-state up front keeps the relationship honest and prevents an indefinite retainer that quietly becomes a permanent cost.

On the legal and operational side, keep it simple but explicit: a written scope of work, defined days or hours, IP and confidentiality terms, a clear communication cadence, and access to the systems and team the CRO needs from day one. A fractional who is fenced off from your CRM, your reps, and your data cannot lead — the most common cause of a failed engagement is not a bad operator but a company that hired one and then withheld the access and authority to actually do the job.

## Related questions
### How much does a fractional CRO cost?
Fractional CROs bill a monthly retainer scaled to days-per-week and pedigree, far below a full-time base-plus-equity package. Get several quotes to triangulate the market rather than anchoring on one figure, and match spend to the outcome required.

### Fractional CRO vs. full-time CRO — which do I need?
Choose fractional when you need to build the revenue machine, install process, and hire your first real sales leader without committing to a permanent six-figure seat. Choose full-time once revenue and headcount justify a dedicated, always-on executive.

### Can a fractional CRO work remotely for an Indiana company?
Yes — the model is video-first with periodic on-site visits, so a strong operator in an adjacent Midwest metro works well. Weight local only when your motion is recruiting-heavy or sells into regional Indiana buyers.

### How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run three to twelve months, structured around building the go-to-market engine and often transitioning to a full-time hire. Multi-month terms with a notice period are standard; open-ended retainers should have milestone checkpoints.

### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant recommends and delivers a report; a fractional CRO owns the number, hires the team, runs the forecast, and executes. You are buying accountable leadership, not advice.

## FAQ
**Where do I start looking for a fractional CRO in Indiana?**
Run five channels in parallel: fractional-executive networks and marketplaces, RevOps consultancies with a fractional tier, warm referrals through Indiana's operator community (TechPoint, Elevate Ventures, founder peer groups), LinkedIn searches filtered to the state, and local professional communities like Pavilion. Referrals and networks take longest, so start them first.

**Does a fractional CRO have to be based in Indiana?**
No. The model is remote-friendly, so operators in Chicago, Cincinnati, Columbus, or Louisville are viable and share the Midwest deal rhythm. Prefer local when your motion depends on recruiting from Indiana talent markets or selling to regional buyers.

**What size company should hire a fractional CRO?**
Typically a growth-stage company past founder-led sales but not yet large enough to justify a full-time CRO's base and equity — often several million in revenue with a small sales team that needs process, leadership, and a hiring plan.

**How do I vet a fractional CRO before signing?**
Build a five-point scorecard (motion fit, stage fit, operating vs. advising, outcome-based references, cultural fit), interview against it, call two or three prior fractional clients, and run a short paid trial diagnostic before committing to a full engagement.

**What should a fractional CRO deliver in the first ninety days?**
A pipeline and forecast audit, an installed or rebuilt sales process, a fixed comp plan, a hiring plan for the roles you actually need, and a reporting cadence the founder and board can trust — with defined milestones at thirty, sixty, and ninety days.

**How is a fractional CRO paid?**
Almost always a monthly retainer tied to committed days per week or a defined scope, on a multi-month term with a notice period. Structure a portion of continuation around hitting milestones rather than paying an open-ended flat fee.

**What are the biggest red flags in a fractional CRO candidate?**
Too many simultaneous clients (attention gets diluted past two or three), promising a revenue number before seeing your pipeline, an all-advisory resume with no recent hands-on operating, and resistance to a paid trial project.

**Can a fractional CRO help us hire our eventual full-time CRO?**
Yes — that transition is often the explicit end goal. A good fractional builds the machine, defines the role, and helps recruit and onboard the permanent leader, then hands off cleanly rather than becoming an indefinite cost.
